near_miss.lead: ox as sacrificial victim: ON leiddi ... oxa gamlan (to Freyr's temple) ~ AVŚ ukṣāṇaṃ ... apacanta (vīrās)
near_miss.why_not: oxi ~ ukṣan is an exact cognate in a sacrificial context, but there is no shared collocation: the Norse leads an old ox to a god's temple and asks for vengeance, the Vedic heroes cook a dappled bull at the first dharmans (cosmic riddle). Bull/ox as victim is generic.

near_miss.lead: ann henni sem augunum í höfði sér 'loves her like the eyes in his head'
near_miss.why_not: Greek partners (Thucydides, Herodotus) have nothing comparable; the best partner is outside the slab (see search lead).

near_miss.lead: weapon + *bʰeyd- + armour: sverd bite ei vápnin ~ (bāṇa) kavacaṃ bhittvā
near_miss.why_not: bíta ~ bhid is cognate and both have a weapon as subject and armour as object, but Gmc 'bite' of blades is a Germanic idiom and 'split the armour' a generic epic battle phrase in Sanskrit; the Þiðreks saga is translated prose. No figure beyond the trivially expected.

near_miss.lead: women at the loom: hǫfðu vef upp fǿrðan ~ ὑφαίνουσι
near_miss.why_not: vefr ~ ὑφαίνω (*webʰ-) only; Herodotus is ethnography of Egyptian men weaving, the Norse the Darraðarljóð valkyrie loom. Shared vocabulary, no shared wording.

near_miss.lead: svaf hann til dagmála ~ ὕπνος ἔμαρπτε
near_miss.why_not: sofa ~ ὕπνος (*swep-) but different syntax (verb vs 'sleep seized him') and different context (sluggard sleeping late vs grieving hero); generic.

near_miss.lead: sváfu þar um nóttina ~ ὕπνος ἔμαρπτε
near_miss.why_not: Itinerary prose 'they slept there that night'; only *swep- shared, no collocation.

near_miss.lead: blood rain as portent: rigndi á þá blóði vellanda
near_miss.why_not: Euripides partner irrelevant; the Greek parallel (Il. 16.459, Hes. Sc. 384) is a motif carried by non-cognate words (see search lead).

near_miss.lead: proverb: þeir menn lifa langan aldr er með orðum eru vegnir
near_miss.why_not: Cato's ham-salting recipe has nothing comparable; 'long life' (langr aldr) has no cognate partner in the bundle.

In Glúmr's stanza sǿtan does not qualify sleep (sofna ek is 'I do not fall asleep'; sǿtan belongs to the reconciliation clause), so no *swéh₂du- + *swep- collocation in the Norse; MBh svādu vyañjanam is food. Lat. suavis sopor alone is not a cross-branch match here.

near_miss.lead: jósu blóði um heraðit allt ~ haurire (fontis)
near_miss.why_not: ausa ~ haurio (*h₂ews-) cognate but the Norse is dream-women sprinkling blood over a district, Lucretius drinking from new springs: no shared context.

near_miss.lead: tears from the eyes: hrutu ór augum honum tár ~ զաչս ... արտասուաց
near_miss.why_not: auga ~ akn, tár ~ artasowkʻ, lacrumas are cognate, but 'tears from eyes' is universal; the Armenian is a quotation of Jeremiah 9:1 (eyes a fountain of tears), the Norse a simile of hail-sized tears. No inherited figure.
Norse 'did not settle (sofnudust) in one place' is not even about sleep; MBh 'did not sleep happily', Lucretius 'to sleep and rest': no shared collocation.

near_miss.lead: 'came at midnight': ad midri nott kiemur ~ uenisti media nocte
near_miss.why_not: Exact triple *médʰyo- + *nókʷt- + *gʷem- in the same syntax, but 'middle of the night' is a compositional, universal time expression that any language keeping these basic words will form (Goth. midjai naht, OE on middre niht, Gk μέσαι νύκτες too); Þiðreks saga is translated from German. Not distinguishable from chance.

near_miss.lead: 'dark night' / 'night darkens' with *merkʷ-: ON nótt er myrk, myrkt af nótt, nótt myrkþi ~ Serb. мркла ноћ, ноћ омркнула ~ Igor Tale ночь мркнетъ
near_miss.why_not: Searched: the collocation is frequent in ON prose (AM-178-fol 2-190:2 nott er myrk; AM-35-fol 237 nótt myrcþi; Egils saga 81r:7 myrkva af nótt), Vuk (21691:613 мркла ноћ; 10118:89 ноћ омркнула) and Igor Tale (spi 33 ночь мркнетъ); myrkr ~ мрак (PGm *merkwa- ~ PSl *mьrk-/*mork-) is a recognised but debated equation. But in each language this is simply the basic word for 'dark' applied to night (byliny renew it as тёмная ночь, OE deorc niht), so the match is generic; and the pivot itself has nott ... myrkt only in parallel clauses, not as a collocation.

near_miss.lead: dregit burst ór nefi 'pull a bristle out of (someone's) nose' (idiom of mocking/injuring)
near_miss.why_not: Irish partner is do greis Conall brod forsin echraid 'urged the goad on the horses': burst and brod are both from *bʰr̥sti-/*bʰrosdʰo- 'point' but the contexts and syntax have nothing in common.

near_miss.lead: hjó í skjǫldinn ok klauf ~ γλύφουσι; Irish cless list
near_miss.why_not: kljúfa ~ γλύφω (*glewbʰ-) only; Herodotus is about carving statues of Pan, the Irish passage a list of Cú Chulainn's feats; shield-splitting is generic battle prose.

near_miss.lead: naming + daughter: nefndi sér vátta ... dóttur ~ θυγάτηρ τε τίθεσθ’ ὄνομ’
near_miss.why_not: nefna ~ ὄνομα, dóttir ~ θυγάτηρ, but the Norse names legal witnesses for a suit over a daughter's dowry, the Greek is Autolykos naming his grandson: different acts, no collocation.

search_lead.cognate: ON auga ~ Lat. oculus (*h₃ekʷ-); verb renewed (unna vs amare)
search_lead.argument: 'to love someone as (more than) one's eyes' in ON saga prose and Catullus, with cognate 'eye' and a renewed love verb. Weak: the comparison is a widespread proverbial endearment and the Latin/biblical 'apple of the eye' (Deut 32:10, Ps 17:8) could have reached Icelandic writers; no Serbian 'kao oko u glavi' found in Vuk to widen it.

search_lead.cognate: none: blóð/αἷμα and rigna/ψιάς are not cognate (motif only)
search_lead.argument: Rain of blood as a portent of a hero's death in battle (Zeus for Sarpedon; Brjáns saga portents before Clontarf in Njála). Congruent context, but carried by non-cognate words, so a motif, not inherited wording; also possibly learned (Christian/classical portent lists).
